title: Why a model should not approve its own actions
lede: The idea behind NEXUS CORE: keep intelligence, authority and execution in separate components.

figure.caption: Authority begins at the boundary. Everything to its left is untrusted proposal.

p: An agent that both proposes and authorizes its own actions collapses two separate questions into one: what should be done, and what is permitted. A language model is a probabilistic function of its context. Its output can be fluent, confident and wrong, and it can be steered by any text that reaches its context window, including files, web pages and user messages.

When authority sits inside that function, a single **adversarial input** or an ordinary mistake is enough to change what the system does. The model's confidence carries no information about whether an action is safe.

NEXUS CORE treats the model as an **untrusted, probabilistic component**. A planner produces a candidate plan, and that plan is data. Authority belongs to a governance stage implemented as ordinary code, whose decisions do not vary with the model's phrasing.

The system executes only what that stage released, through a layer that cannot be talked into doing more. The trust boundary sits between proposal and decision, which is where the trust actually changes.

A policy engine evaluates each proposed step against explicit rules and returns a decision such as allow, deny or hold for approval. **Determinism** is the point: the same plan under the same policy produces the same decision, so rules can be unit tested, reviewed in a diff and changed deliberately.
A control that depends on how a prompt happens to be worded cannot be tested in that sense. A control expressed as code can.

Sensitive operations, including financial actions, are designed to enter a **held state**. Leaving that state requires an approval event that originates outside the model, so a persuasive explanation inside a model response cannot satisfy it.
The principle behind it is simple. A response that claims an action was authorized, or that it happened, is not evidence of either. Evidence is a state transition in the system, written down.

Governance decisions and executions are written to an audit record using **audit hashes**. Chaining records makes silent modification detectable, which turns the history into something that can be verified instead of trusted.
This also changes debugging. When a run behaves unexpectedly, the question becomes which stage made which decision, and the record answers it.
A corrector stage examines execution results and intermediate state for errors. It is deliberately bounded: it may propose repairs, and every repair re-enters the same governance path.
Without that constraint, error recovery would become a second, unreviewed route to authority, which is exactly the property the architecture is trying to remove.

The separation adds components, state and latency, and each extra stage is more code to test. It does not make a model correct. It **narrows what an incorrect model can do** and makes failures attributable to a stage.
This note describes design intent. It makes no claim about test results or production readiness.

title: NEXUS CORE, end to end
lede: How a request moves through a governance-first agent prototype: what is real, what is simulated and what is still planned.

figure.caption: The model proposes a plan. A separate, deterministic layer decides whether anything runs, and every stage leaves a record.

p: NEXUS CORE treats a language model as an untrusted, probabilistic engine. The model can interpret a request, choose an approach, propose tool calls and revise a rejected plan. It cannot authorize its own proposal: every plan passes through a deterministic, **fail-closed** policy check before anything executes.

This note describes the current working prototype. It is a governance-first orchestration pipeline in active development, not a finished sandbox or a production-ready autonomous platform. Where something is simulated or only planned, the note says so.

The interface is a Next.js and React Command Center where users submit tasks, inspect conversations, watch pipeline events and review governance decisions. It reads a Server-Sent Events stream, so blocked decisions and the correction loop are visible instead of hidden behind a single answer.

A FastAPI backend exposes authentication, projects, conversations, messages, task streaming, artifacts and audit records. It validates request bodies, resolves who is calling and hands orchestration to one orchestrator. A demo identity exists for development. It is not an acceptable default for a multi-user deployment.

Before planning, the orchestrator passes up to the last 20 messages to a semantic understanding step that infers intent, task type, complexity, ambiguity and security signals, with a fallback if the model is unavailable. A separate pattern classifier checks the original input for instruction overrides, prompt extraction, fake system messages and obfuscation. These signals inform the plan and add defense in depth. They are evidence, not authorization.

A router maps the task to a category, model configuration and reasoning mode, using semantic hints with a keyword fallback. The planner agent, ELLA, then turns the request into a structured execution plan: a summary, a response mode and ordered steps, each with an action, a target, parameters and a rationale.

Governance evaluates that plan. If it is blocked, a correction agent, JANE, may revise it. Approved plans reach the execution layer, which dispatches supported actions and collects logs and artifacts. SQLite stores projects, conversations, messages, tasks, artifacts and the audit records.

A request starts in the frontend and opens a streaming endpoint. The orchestrator creates a task record, loads earlier messages and stores the new user message. Semantic understanding and the security classifier run, the router picks a category, and the planner proposes a structured plan that is parsed and validated against a shared schema.

Governance then evaluates the plan independently of the planner. A blocked plan may go to the correction agent, and the revised plan must pass governance again. Repeated rejection ends the task. An approved plan is executed, results and artifacts are collected, and the response and task state are saved. Each stage is streamed to the client as it completes and written to the audit record.
One honest edge: when a client disconnects, the pipeline stops advancing, but a model request that is already in flight cannot be guaranteed to stop immediately.

sections.h: A plan that parses is not a plan that is safe
p: Model output goes through defensive JSON extraction and schema validation before it becomes a plan. That establishes structure only. A well-formed plan can still ask for something dangerous, which is why validation and authorization are separate steps.

The planner also has three response modes: answer directly, ask for clarification without inventing steps, or execute tools. The distinction keeps a vague request from being turned into confident-looking actions.

The governance layer is plain Python rules, not another model asked whether the plan seems safe. It inspects the flattened content of each step for dangerous system commands, destructive SQL, sensitive file paths, path traversal and secret exfiltration, and it rejects blocked action names. The result is a structured verdict: the decision, the rules that fired, the security signals and a reason.
If evaluation itself throws an exception, the verdict is **blocked**, never implicit approval. The same input and configuration give the same decision, and a rejection always names its reason.
The limit matters just as much: a pattern-based evaluator is only as complete as its patterns. It is not a full policy language and not proof of safety.

When a plan is blocked, the correction agent receives the rejected plan and the governance feedback and tries again. Its output is more model-generated data, so it is parsed, validated and evaluated exactly like the original. Without that rule, the correction path would be a bypass around the policy boundary.

The loop is bounded, with a default maximum of two correction attempts, so a stubborn plan ends in rejection instead of retrying forever. It does not provide human approval, rollback or protection against partial effects from future real integrations.

sections.h: What is simulated, and why it matters
p: Most actions in the prototype are simulated. Read-only web search is the one documented real external tool. Importing a tool module does not mean its action has a production-safe execution path.

The distinction matters because a simulated file write shows orchestration behavior. It does not prove filesystem isolation, and a governance verdict is not a replacement for a separate permission check at the real tool boundary. The code also sanitizes search results and classifies known injection patterns. Those are supporting defenses, not proof that hostile content is neutralized.

sections.h: An audit trail with honest limits
p: Each stage writes an append-oriented audit record: the task, stage, label, details, a timestamp, the previous record's hash and its own SHA-256 hash. The event stream carries the record hash, so the interface can show a hash-linked timeline and whether the chain verifies. Deleting a conversation or a message does not touch the audit tables, so the execution history can outlive the content.

Hash linking detects some kinds of tampering. It does not make the database immutable, because someone who can rewrite the records can recompute the chain. Stronger integrity would need independent checkpoints or signatures.

sections.h: A bug worth telling: timestamps that sort wrong
p: Timestamps were stored as text, and Python's default ISO format drops the fractional seconds when the microseconds are exactly zero. Mixed representations then sort and compare unexpectedly as strings. That affects message order and any operation that deletes a message and everything after it.

The fix is to always serialize with explicit microsecond precision, so every stored timestamp has the same shape and text order matches time order. No separate regression test for this is claimed yet.

Built in the prototype: the API and Command Center, structured plans with shared schemas, semantic understanding and prompt classification, routing, the planner and correction agents, fail-closed governance, bounded correction with re-evaluation, SSE pipeline events, SQLite persistence, hash-linked audit records with chain verification, multi-turn context, full-text message search where the SQLite runtime supports it, and mostly simulated execution with one real read-only search path.

Still planned or incomplete: enforced production authentication with verified isolation between users, authorization enforced at each real tool boundary, a general human-approval workflow, real integrations with scoped permissions, complete automated security and regression tests, independent audit checkpoints, rate limiting and monitoring, and embedding-based memory in place of today's full-text search.

The first priority is making authorization an execution invariant: a typed contract between governance and execution, so every real tool call traces back to the exact approved action, target and parameters, and anything unknown or malformed is rejected by default.

After that come reproducible security tests that record false positives and false negatives, lifecycle failure tests for timeouts, disconnects and corrupted audit chains, one narrowly scoped real integration with every allowed, blocked, denied and failed path tested, signed audit checkpoints, and reliability baselines before any scaling decisions. The longer plan is in the next note.

title: Where NEXUS CORE goes next
lede: A planned roadmap for durable missions, governed multi-agent work and approvals, with the safety primitives built first.

figure.caption: Safety and reliability primitives come first. Autonomy expands only inside enforceable authority.

p: Everything in this note is a planned extension. None of it is a claim about the current implementation, which is a request-and-response orchestration prototype. The architecture note says what exists today.

The principle does not change: models are **untrusted probabilistic engines**. Autonomy decides how independently a mission progresses. It never gives a model control over the rules that authorize its actions.

The order is deliberate. First come execution-boundary authorization and typed capability contracts. Then a durable mission runtime with checkpoints, cancellation and recovery. Then governed multi-agent coordination with independent verification, followed by approval workflows and explicit autonomy levels, then persistent memory and mission-wide tracing, and only then broader tool integrations.
The order may change as testing exposes dependencies. What should not change is the rule behind it: expand the ability to act only after the controls around acting are enforced and tested.

Today a task is one request and one plan. The plan is to move to missions with an explicit lifecycle: objectives, constraints, deadlines, completion criteria and cancellation. Work would be split into dependency-aware graphs, run by persistent workers with checkpoints, retries and timeouts.

A mission could pause for missing information, a policy decision or human approval, then resume from recorded state. Scheduled and event-triggered runs would carry bounded retries and resource budgets.

Specialized agents would handle planning, research, coding, testing, analysis, security review, execution and verification, coordinated by an agent that delegates work, tracks dependencies and decides when a mission is done. Contracts between agents would be typed, and one agent's output is treated as untrusted input to the next, even inside the same system.
Agents cannot grant themselves permissions or change their own authority boundaries. Specialization must never create an ungoverned execution path.

sections.h: A capability layer instead of wired-in tools
p: Individually wired tools would give way to a registry and an execution gateway. Each capability declares its parameters, required permissions, side effects, risk class and limits. Authorization is enforced at the execution boundary, not only when the plan is made, with least-privilege credentials, target restrictions, quotas, timeouts and isolation per capability. Invocations are recorded with secrets redacted.
Having a tool never implies unrestricted authority to use it.

Four levels are planned. Advisory returns recommendations and executes nothing. Supervised prepares and validates plans, then asks for approval before designated actions. Bounded autonomous executes permitted actions within configured permissions, budgets and targets. Mission-based pursues a persistent objective through many governed steps and stops or asks for help when it reaches a boundary.

The exact permission model and the transitions between levels are still to be designed. Governance would judge the actual action, target, parameters and current authority, never the model's explanation of its intent.

sections.h: Approval that binds to what was reviewed
p: An approval request would carry the proposed action, the affected resources, a risk class, the rationale and the evidence, with approve, reject, cancel, pause and resume. An approval would be bound to the exact plan version that was reviewed and invalidated when something material changes.
A rejection or a policy violation can never be quietly reinterpreted as permission to continue. A governance APPROVED verdict stays distinct from a human decision.

Short-term conversation, mission state, long-term memory and retrieved reference material would be kept apart. Semantic retrieval with embeddings, and possibly graph relationships, would sit beside today's text search. Every stored item would carry provenance, ownership and access control, and the system would tell observed facts, user instructions, inferences and unverified agent output apart.
Memory can inform a decision. It must not silently expand authority or override a higher-priority control.

sections.h: Verification that does not trust the worker
p: Acceptance criteria would be defined before execution where possible, checked by independent reviewers or deterministic validators. The system would ask for evidence of completion instead of accepting a successful tool response or a confident claim. Disagreement between planner, executor and verifier goes to correction or to a person.

Verification results would be stored separately from the claims of the agent that did the work, and adversarial tests would cover prompt injection, malicious tool results, parameter manipulation and attempts to bypass governance.

JANE would grow from plan correction into security monitoring: correlating events across agents and missions, spotting repeated blocks, escalation attempts and abnormal resource use, and suspending a mission at configured thresholds. It could report and recommend, but it must not rewrite the rules that constrain it.

Audit would gain mission-wide traces, cost and latency tracking, and externally anchored or signed checkpoints, because hash links alone do not stop someone who can rewrite the database. The interface would grow from a conversation view into mission control: execution graphs, live traces, approval queues, permissions and budgets, showing what the system is doing and why.

Beyond that are controlled software-development and deployment workflows, browser and application automation, and, where proper safety systems exist, device control. Each needs its own threat model, tests and safeguards. None is implied by today's simulated tools.
The long-term goal is a persistent, multi-agent automation system that can plan, act, observe, verify, recover and keep working toward objectives inside explicit, enforceable authority boundaries.

title: Lagoon, end to end
lede: A social operating system built from a modular frontend and a real edge backend, with an honest map of what is live and what is simulated.

figure.caption: The app runs fully on the device. Signing in swaps selected simulated features for real services.

sections.h: What Lagoon is trying to be
p: Lagoon is a social operating system built around communication, relationships, content, communities, information and personal productivity. It is not meant to be another feed-first network. The direction is relationship-oriented rather than engagement-oriented: connect people, their conversations, their interests and what they want to get done.

The idea is one environment where people can communicate privately, keep relationships and communities, share media, discover information, read, watch, learn and create, organize their conversations and activities, and use an integrated assistant. Communication is the foundation, but it is not the limit.

sections.h: A frontend built from registered modules
p: The frontend is custom modular JavaScript, not a React or Next.js application. Numbered modules share one application namespace with common state, an event bus, feature registries, navigation and screen management, shared interface components, a shell and theme system, and a boot layer.

Features plug in through small registration calls for tabs, screens, attachments, settings, message types, chat actions, quick actions and shells, instead of being written into one enormous file. That gives Lagoon a plugin-like internal structure without a separate package per feature.

sections.h: A build step that enforces rules
p: A build script collects the CSS and JavaScript from the source folder, sorts modules by filename, merges the CSS, keeps each JavaScript file as its own script tag so a syntax error stays isolated to one module, checks syntax, rejects em dashes and en dashes, and emits a self-contained HTML app.
One caution: older flat files sit beside the source folder as a parallel layout. Only the source folder is built, so the two must not be treated as interchangeable.

Cloudflare Workers handle the HTTP requests. D1 holds the relational data, Durable Objects hold live connections and shared counters, server-side AI runs on the same platform, and a separate hosted service executes remote code. An Inbox object manages one user's active WebSocket connections and event delivery.
An older room object is explicitly retired and answers with HTTP 410. Lagoon should not be described as having a room-based messaging service.

sections.h: Local first, live when signed in
p: The app works locally with simulated conversations, messages, status changes and persistence. When a user signs in, selected features are replaced or extended by real services. So not every screen is a live capability: some are simulated, some live, some both, and some are in test mode.
Keeping demo state and live state strictly separate is a design rule, and the main thing the next stage should consolidate.

There are 25 shells, from Glass, Material and Bento to Editorial, Swiss, Terminal and two iOS variants. A shell is not a color preset. It can change navigation, layout, component shapes, typography, density, motion, light and dark themes, chat bubbles, lists, sheets, cards and responsive behavior. One feature implementation inherits every treatment without being rewritten.

Browser tests run at phone, tablet and desktop sizes and collect page and console errors, screenshots, shell audits, overflow and contrast checks and feature tests, across 36 frontend test files. Nine backend scripts cover authentication and general API behavior, messaging, WebSocket delivery, avatars, the assistant, code execution, public data adapters, privacy and social features. Some target the live API and others run against isolated local environments.

Honest limits: the existence of tests is not the same as passing them, and a code review is not a fresh run of the suite. The package's default test command is also a placeholder, so no single command runs everything yet.

title: Two trust models in one product
lede: Sealed one-to-one chats, per-member sealed groups and readable, moderated Spaces: different promises for different places, stated plainly.

figure.caption: In private chats the server sees sealed envelopes. In moderated Spaces it deliberately sees readable text. The product says which is which.

p: A private conversation and a moderated community need opposite things. A private chat should be unreadable to the service. A community needs moderation, and moderation needs the service to see content. Lagoon keeps both and does not blur them.
Space messages are readable on the service so they can be moderated. They are **not end-to-end encrypted**, and the product should never imply that they are.

sections.h: One to one: sealed on the device
p: A dedicated module uses the browser's cryptographic APIs: ECDH on P-256 for key agreement, HKDF with SHA-256 and HMAC-based derivation, and AES-GCM for encryption. Device keys live in IndexedDB. Public keys and prekeys are published, and the module handles session state, safety codes, encrypted files, and encrypted key backup and restore. It also contains ratchet-related logic and a prekey handshake.
The service stores message records in D1, but the client is built so that it receives sealed content rather than readable private text. This is a substantial implementation, not an encryption icon.
Cryptographic code is not an audit. The protocol has not been independently reviewed, and strong security guarantees should wait until it has been.

The live path covers phone-number account lookup, sending, synchronization, delivery acknowledgements, history and live events over WebSockets. A per-user Inbox object holds the connections and delivers events.

For groups, the sending device seals each message separately for each member. The server keeps membership and roles and relays the encrypted envelopes. The backend covers creation, invitations, joining and leaving, member management, roles, editing, sync, delivery acknowledgements, read state, reports and moderation workflows.
Group encryption should not automatically be credited with every property of the one-to-one protocol.

Spaces are invite-based environments with members, roles, text channels, channel permissions, reports, moderation, automated moderation rules, adult-channel restrictions and invite management. Communities are named groups with membership and an announcement feed controlled by owners and administrators.
Channels are one-to-many broadcasting: creation, a directory, following, posts, reactions, polls, reports and deletion. Followers pull the feed instead of the system pushing to each of them.

Images, video, voice messages, documents and view-once media are uploaded in chunks, kept locally in IndexedDB and fetched on demand. The backend stores the chunks in D1 rather than in object storage. The limits in code are 384 KB per chunk, 25 MB per file and 200 MB of uploads per person per day.
That reduces infrastructure for now, but database-backed media deserves a dedicated scaling review.

There are two call paths: a simulated local experience and a live WebRTC implementation. The server handles signalling, call logs and ICE configuration while audio and video travel peer to peer. The live path is for individual calls. Group-call screens that exist in the simulated experience should not be presented as a finished live feature.

title: Ella proposes, the app decides
lede: How an in-app assistant can be useful without being handed the keys: layered reasoning, an action allowlist and model output treated as data, not markup.

figure.caption: The model can suggest an action or a layout. The application checks it against a fixed allowlist before anything happens or renders.

p: Ella, Lagoon's integrated assistant, is built in layers. It is not a chat box attached to an API, and each layer has its own limits.

A local layer needs no network and no language model. It handles calculations, unit conversions, reminders, to-dos, timers, memory, message checking, rewriting and conversation summaries. A router decides whether a request stays local or goes to a remote service, and it can use public data services for selected information requests.

Server routes cover chat, image generation and understanding, search, link fetching, research, speech, transcription and translation-related work. They run on the same edge platform and have daily usage limits.

A set of public data adapters each talk to a fixed, known host and include health checks. That is a deliberate choice: known sources mean a user-supplied address cannot become an unrestricted server fetch.

Users can configure their own language model providers. This path supports streaming responses, tool execution and conversation context with consent controls, and it is separate from the free server-side path.

sections.h: Knowing the app without controlling it
p: The agent layer learns Lagoon's real screens, settings and actions from the same registries the app uses. Its actions come from a fixed allowlist, so a model-generated instruction cannot become an arbitrary application operation. The documented restrictions exclude actions that involve money, accounts or other people.

The model can return data that describes supported interface components, and the frontend alone decides how to render them. Text is escaped, links must be HTTPS and actions must be on the allowlist. The model proposes content. It never gets to inject HTML into the app.
Multi-step tasks, durable task state, background continuation, approvals and a visible execution history are planned, not built. They are described in the roadmap note.

title: Running code in two sandboxes
lede: A browser-side Linux emulator and a remote runner are different environments with different boundaries.

figure.caption: Different jobs, different boundaries: one runs inside the browser, the other on a separate service that trusts only signed requests.

p: Lagoon can run code in two places, and they should never be confused. One is an emulated Linux environment inside the browser. The other is a remote runner on a separate service.

A PC emulator boots a BusyBox environment inside a sandboxed iframe. The design intent is a guest with no network access, no access to Lagoon's own pages and a separate environment that runs shell scripts and forgets everything afterwards. The emulator files ship with the backend's public assets.

The runner is a separate Deno service. Requests to it are signed with HMAC, carry a timestamp and a nonce, and are checked for replay. It limits code length, output size and execution time, runs one job at a time with restricted permissions in temporary job directories, and uses Pyodide for Python. The Worker also runs static checks on code before dispatching it.
The repository has offline guard tests and a separate probe script for the sandbox. As elsewhere, having them is not the same as having run them for this note.

The emulator keeps code inside the user's own browser. The remote runner offers more power under stricter control. They answer different threats, and both are described here by what the code does, not by any certification.

title: Six surfaces, one app
lede: Stories, Snap, Reels, Channels, the Library and personal Spaces: what each one is and how much of it is live.

figure.caption: Many experiences have both a local simulation and a live backend. The notes name which is which.

p: Lagoon has several distinct social and content systems. Some are real backend services, some are local simulations, and some use both depending on sign-in. Each is described below by what exists.
A local story experience sits beside a live status service. The live service supports publishing, audience settings, feeds, views, reactions, viewer lists, resharing and deletion.

Snap is a separate identity and sharing subsystem with usernames, friend relationships, snaps, view-once delivery, opened and viewed state, streaks, stories with expiry and friend discovery. Live state is kept apart from demo data.
Reels is real short video backed by the server: uploads, a feed, views, likes, saves, following creators, comments and comment deletion, creator profiles, video streaming and content rating checks.
Channels are one-to-many broadcasts with a directory, following, posts, reactions, polls and reports. Followers pull the feed rather than relying on push fan-out.

The Library offers free public-domain books from fixed public sources. Readers can search inside a book, bookmark, customize the reader, keep opened books offline and ask the assistant about passages. Watch offers selected open-licence and public-domain media, including curated Internet Archive collections, open films and Wikimedia Commons material. It is not a subscription streaming service.

Personal Spaces is a local environment, calculated on the device: search across conversations and people, personal chat groupings, relationship activity, conversation timelines, plans detected in messages, notes, and export and restore. It must not be confused with the server-backed community Spaces.
Discover covers people, trends and content. The backend supplies real, data-derived trending and creator information, while some discovery and creator experiences still use local presentation logic.

title: Safety, privacy and what is not finished
lede: Age checks, guardian consent, privacy rules enforced on the server and reporting with appeals, plus a plain statement of the work left before a public launch.

figure.caption: Privacy and age rules are enforced on the backend, so a modified client cannot skip them.

p: The privacy system controls last-seen visibility, active status, read receipts, profile visibility, audience restrictions, blocking and contact-based access. These are enforced on the backend, not only hidden in the interface, so a modified client cannot skip them.

The backend determines age from date of birth, restricts minor accounts and limits adult-to-minor interaction. A guardian flow handles onboarding, confirmation, consent records and management, with optional identity review. An uploaded image is kept for human review and deleted after a decision.
This is a significant safety implementation. It still needs a production-grade operational and legal process around it.
Users, groups, Spaces and advertisements can be reported. Administrators review reports, can suspend accounts with a recorded reason, and appeals are supported. Actions leave audit records.
People can export their data, delete their account, list and revoke sessions (sessions last 30 days), send feedback and manage devices.

A guard module rate-limits with local counters and with shared counters held in Durable Objects, alongside platform-level protections. How it behaves when the shared counters are unavailable still needs failure testing.

Business features include profiles, catalogues, public pages, greeting, away and quick-reply messages, opt-in customer relationships with broadcast quotas, and reservations. Greeting and away behavior run on the device while the app is open.

Advertising is explicitly in test mode: advertiser accounts, test credits, campaigns and review, impression and click tracking, frequency controls and hide and report options. It is designed to show ads only to adults whose age is known and to avoid personalization. It is not a production payment system.

Lagoon is a substantial working system, not a production-certified service. Hardening of sign-in and verification, network policy, independent cryptographic review, legal documents, access-control audits, backup and restore tests, load tests and monitoring are all still ahead. The roadmap note lists them.

title: Where Lagoon goes next
lede: Consolidate and harden first, then connect what already exists before adding more.

figure.caption: Consolidate and harden first. Then connect what exists before adding more.

p: Everything in this note is planned. None of it is a claim about what exists today. The next stage should not be about adding features indiscriminately.

sections.h: First, make demo versus live honest
p: Some screens are simulated, some are live and some are in test mode. The first job is to make that distinction consistent in the product and to keep the frontend and backend contracts in step.

Before a broad public launch: replace test-mode behavior with production behavior, tighten network and origin policy, complete the legal review, have the cryptography independently reviewed, test the guardian and age workflows, audit access control on every backend route, verify that data export and deletion are complete, test backup and restore, run load tests, set up monitoring and incident response, and verify that deployed bundles match the intended source revision.

Grow the relationship graph beyond contacts and followers: relationship context, shared interests, important interactions, conversation continuity, personal relationship spaces and insights the user controls. It must help people manage relationships without turning private interactions into a surveillance mechanism.

A person should be able to say what they want: learn something, find someone, create something, organize an activity, continue a conversation, research a subject or plan an event. Lagoon should understand the destination and the context instead of treating every request as a search or a chat message.

A conversation could become a plan, a plan a reminder, a reminder could link to a relevant Space, and a shared resource could enter the Library, with the assistant helping organize it. All of it would run through explicit permissions and user-controlled context sharing.

The assistant would grow from application actions toward multi-step tasks, durable task state, background continuation, better tool orchestration, verification, recovery from failures, permission tiers, human approval for consequential actions and a clear execution history. It should not receive unrestricted authority just because it can call tools.

One search across people, chats, messages, groups, Spaces, communities, channels, reels, the Library and saved information, respecting each subsystem's access rules. A personal knowledge environment with notes, collections, saved resources, timelines and user-controlled export. Better collaboration, event coordination, shared plans, moderation tools and roles for communities. And for creators, analytics, publishing workflows, scheduling, audience insights, discovery and production-grade monetization.

Evaluate object storage and lifecycle management for media, database indexing and query performance, background jobs, more resilient event delivery, observability, backups and recovery, automated deployment checks, and load and concurrency testing. Database-backed media storage works today but needs its own scaling strategy.

title: ELLA, end to end
lede: How a WhatsApp assistant is built so the chat app is only a transport, with an honest account of what is verified and what is not.

figure.caption: A message is normalized before it enters the pipeline. Tool use passes through policy checks, never straight from the model.

sections.h: WhatsApp is a transport, not the application
p: ELLA is a modular, natural-language-first WhatsApp assistant built around NEXUS CORE. ELLA is the conversational face. NEXUS coordinates understanding, context, intent routing, policy checks, tools and the shape of the reply. The aim is a practical interface to useful AI capabilities without making the language model the authority over what the system may do.

Incoming messages are normalized before they reach the conversational pipeline, so nothing downstream depends on WhatsApp's raw format. The project is in active development: working paths sit beside partly connected and planned ones, and code existing in the repository does not by itself mean its production workflow has been verified.

A linked WhatsApp session receives the message, which is normalized and passed through activation and context resolution. NEXUS then detects intent, decides whether a clarifying question is needed, builds a bounded plan, evaluates authorization and tool policy, runs tools through typed contracts, validates their output, composes the reply, and records memory, audit events and telemetry.

The tools themselves are typed and registered: chat replies, image generation and analysis, transcription, speech, web search, document questions and more. A tool being technically able to run is never the same as being permitted to.

sections.h: Context that applies only when it applies
p: Quoted messages, attachments, chat history and group references inform a reply only when they bear on the current request. WhatsApp embeds the message being replied to, so replying to an old photo with a short instruction can act on that photo.

Routing is attachment-aware before any text heuristics run: an image goes to vision, a voice note is transcribed and then answered, a document is ingested or queried. When wording and attachment both point somewhere, explicit intent such as asking for a sticker wins over plain image analysis.

Each linked account gets its own bot session. Shared infrastructure such as the model gateway, tools and memory is injected, while per-session state lives on the session itself. Every chat, document and memory lookup is scoped by account and chat, so two linked numbers never see each other's data even when they share a store.

Accounts use hashed passwords and opaque bearer tokens. The dashboard, plain HTML and JavaScript, handles signup, linking by QR code or pairing code, and settings. A few behaviors are explicit opt-in toggles: AI replies, automatic reactions, automatic read receipts, an always-online presence and re-posting deleted text.

Supabase holds selected account, session and persistence data, with migrations for persistence, WhatsApp session leases, account capability preferences, game sessions, web history and artifact metadata. Other parts still use JSON files or memory.
That means durability and horizontal scaling are not uniform across subsystems. Moving to one deliberate source of truth is part of the target architecture, covered in the roadmap note.

sections.h: A web workspace beside the bot
p: A separate React and Vite web app hosts the research, scraping and agent tools, on top of the same account system. The next notes cover how those tools are kept safe.

Behavior is checked by about fifty standalone test scripts plus package tests, chained by the main test command: intent routing, media fetch, response guard, tool registry, conversation understanding, group references, call state, the agent platform and more. Many run against fake providers.

The project's own principle applies here: smoke-tested logic, live-provider behavior and end-to-end production workflows are different levels of verification. These tests were not re-run for this note.

title: Capability is not authority, in a chat
lede: What changes when an assistant lives inside group chats: risk-tiered roles, untrusted everything, and a last check before every reply.

figure.caption: The model may request a tool. A separate check on the actor's role and the tool's risk decides whether it runs.

p: Capability does not imply authority. The model may request a tool, but it does not authorize it, and NEXUS never treats model-generated tool selection as permission. Authorization happens downstream, independently of what the planner chose.

There are five roles, from owner down through super admin, admin and moderator to user, and four risk levels. Low and medium risk tools are open to any user, high risk needs at least a moderator, and critical needs an admin. A critical tool still asks for approval unless the actor is the owner, because a role that clears the bar is still not blanket authority.
The role lookup is in memory today, with a store-backed lookup planned. The gate is real, and it is also still a first version.

External messages, attachments, retrieved web pages, documents and model output are all treated as untrusted. The threat model names the risks plainly: direct and indirect prompt injection, excessive agency, privilege escalation, unauthorized group and admin actions, data leaking across users or groups, SSRF through URL tools, arbitrary code execution, malicious files, unbounded AI consumption, secrets leaking into prompts or logs, an insecure plugin supply chain, injection into queries and commands, and replayed or duplicate messages.

Least privilege for every tool. Typed schemas and strict validation. Per-user and per-group scope. Explicit approval for high-impact actions. Sandboxed code with no network. URL allow and deny policies. File type and size limits. Rate limits and quotas. Audit logs. Redaction of secrets in logs. Timeouts and resource limits. And adversarial tests for prompt injection.

sections.h: Where documents and code can disagree
p: The README says it directly: do not assume a documented control is implemented simply because it appears in an architecture or threat-model document. The threat model states intended controls. How far each one is implemented varies, which is why the project asks readers to review authorization and account isolation before exposing the API publicly.

sections.h: A last check on the way out
p: A response guard runs immediately before every user-facing send: HTTP replies, streamed replies, WhatsApp messages, media captions and even fallback and error messages. It drops internal diagnostic lines, removes provider and model identifiers so they stay in server-side diagnostics, replaces secret-shaped strings with a redaction marker and trims canned assistant boilerplate. It is defense in depth, not the primary control.

title: From a link to an answer, safely
lede: Four request types kept apart, URL rules that assume hostile input, and research whose citations can be checked.

figure.caption: A pasted link, a search, a supplied file and a generation request are different jobs with different rules.

p: A request that involves the web can be web research, a search for an existing public-domain or licensed asset, a fetch of one explicit public link, or generation. Intent precedence keeps them apart. A bare link on a recognized platform is a fetch request. An ordinary article link stays web research. Searching for an existing asset stays asset search, and generation stays generation.

One fetch pipeline handles direct public HTTPS files and public links on an exact allowlist of platforms. It has distinct modes for downloading, extracting audio, transcribing and analyzing, runs a pinned version of the extractor, and has focused tests for intent collisions and retries.

sections.h: URL rules that assume hostile input
p: Opening a URL blocks embedded credentials, unusual ports, local, private and reserved addresses, unsupported schemes and unsafe redirects. Page content is untrusted and cannot override instructions or permissions.

Two honest caveats are written into the project. Network egress restrictions are still recommended on top of application checks, and DNS rebinding between validation and connection is a residual risk that application code alone cannot remove.

Search results must come from live provider output, because a model's answer is not proof of a search. Every source-specific claim needs a direct URL. Publication date is not retrieval time, and a missing date stays missing. A failed search must not trigger a roundup made up from memory. A claim of a screenshot requires a real image, and song lookups return legal listening links and short previews, not downloads.

Image and video search gathers candidates across providers, removes duplicates by source page and ranks them on titles, tags, descriptions and the original request. Poor metadata matches are rejected, and when nothing fits the answer is a not-found result, not a random picture. The check is metadata-based, not pixel-level, and the docs say so. Captions say a result was retrieved, never generated.

The web workspace adds a scraper with bounded extraction, sitemap discovery, focused crawling and quote-verified field extraction, and a research mode that plans, searches, reads, takes quote-backed notes, checks for gaps, writes a cited report and checks citations sentence by sentence. Citation checking is not a truth guarantee, and the system says so.

Autonomous agent tasks run under step, page, model and time budgets and can pause, resume, cancel and ask for approval. Crawls over 15 pages need approval, and in assisted mode every sandbox run does too. Fetched pages are treated as untrusted data, and the note-taking steps that read them have no tools. Robots rules are honoured.
These routes are off unless explicitly switched on, and the docs say not to enable them on a public host until network egress blocks private and metadata address ranges.

title: Behaving like a guest on WhatsApp
lede: A bot on a consumer messaging network has to avoid looking like a bot, and has to be honest that no amount of care guarantees it.

labels: Read and type like a person
figure.caption: Every pattern that makes automation easy to spot is a reason to slow it down.

p: ELLA lives on a consumer messaging network that can remove accounts that look automated. It reaches WhatsApp through an unofficial client library, so continuity of an account cannot be promised by this project or by anyone.

The session layer ramps up gradually after a new link, never starts a conversation on its own, and delays reading and typing with randomized, human-shaped timing. Pacing follows the time of day, rapid messages are debounced into one reply, and a health score tracks how the account is behaving.

Instant read receipts and a constantly online presence are themselves detectable patterns. They exist as opt-in toggles for people who want them, not as defaults, and the settings page says why next to each one.

The README is blunt: anti-ban timing and humanization features do not guarantee that WhatsApp will permit or preserve an account. External providers and unofficial integrations can change or fail independently of the repository.

title: Many models, one voice
lede: A gateway that routes, falls back and keeps credentials tidy, with a final layer that keeps the assistant sounding like one assistant.

figure.caption: Providers come and go. The gateway routes around failures, and the user hears one consistent assistant.

p: Provider adapters cover chat, vision, transcription, image generation, speech and search. A model registry, a capability registry and task routing decide which provider handles a request, and a fallback chain moves on when one fails or is unavailable. Several adapters are free or keyless, which keeps the system usable without paid keys.

Fallback is ordered and the gateway tracks provider health, so a failing provider is skipped instead of retried forever. Providers can change or break independently of the project. The design treats that as normal.
A credential store holds named keys, and values set in the environment win over keys stored through the dashboard. Admin tools manage the stored ones.

A language layer handles Nigerian English and Pidgin, alongside modules for conversation tone, conversation state and understanding. The goal is replies that fit how people actually write, including fragments and abbreviations, instead of rigid helpdesk phrasing.

An identity layer keeps the assistant's persona consistent. Provider and model identifiers stay in server diagnostics and are scrubbed from user-facing text, and response-quality checks treat requests for current availability or factual verification with extra care, so the assistant does not answer them from memory alone.

title: More than a chatbot
lede: Games, an economy, guilds, collectibles and group tools: the social layer that makes a chat assistant worth keeping in a group.

figure.caption: The same pipeline that answers questions also runs games, tracks balances and handles group chores.

p: A registry of more than 200 named games is built from interactive engines such as Connect Four, Blackjack and Memory Match, plus content packs for trivia. Game results feed an economy with wallets, a bank, experience and levels, daily rewards, a shop and inventory, and a leaderboard. Everything is reachable in plain language, such as asking for a balance or to play a game.

Guilds with shared experience, away messages that reply when someone is mentioned, a card collection with rarity weights, and virtual pets sit beside native WhatsApp polls and a set of small utilities. A note on game moves covers keeping them safe from abuse.

In groups, ELLA replies to mentions, parses admin commands deterministically instead of asking the model, has link and spam moderation paths, and supports welcome and goodbye templates. Group activation rules decide when it speaks at all, which matters more in a busy group than in a private chat.
Persistence for these features is not uniform, and some parts depend on live participant data from WhatsApp. They are described here as present in the code, not as verified in every group.

title: Where ELLA goes next
lede: A target architecture for durable work, with the current implementation and the plan kept deliberately separate.

figure.caption: The target state is a plan. The current state is the single process described in the other notes.

p: This note describes target-state components, not claims that they are connected or production-ready. The project's own documents say the design material still has to be reconciled with the running implementation.

PostgreSQL would become the source of truth for persistent data, replacing today's mix of Supabase tables, JSON files and memory. Vector search would be added only where semantic retrieval is justified and evaluated, not by default.

Redis with a job queue would carry long-running tasks, handled by explicit worker processes with retries, idempotency, cancellation and result delivery. S3-compatible object storage would hold larger media and generated artifacts.

sections.h: Visibility and the order of work
p: Structured observability, wider audit coverage and operational health checks come with it. The roadmap runs from a thin vertical slice, through persistence, a tool registry with permissions and audit, media pipelines, research and memory, queues and schedulers, group moderation and policies, plugins and an admin dashboard, sandboxed coding with approvals, and finally security testing, load testing, backups and deployment hardening.

title: Sending a message to the right place
lede: Intent routing in a WhatsApp assistant, and why a message that looks like a command is not one.

figure.caption: Routing is a decision made from intent and conversation state, not a lookup on keywords.

p: Messaging traffic is short, fragmentary and context-dependent. People mix languages, abbreviate, and answer a question asked ten messages ago. Treating each message as an isolated string to match against keywords produces a system that is brittle in exactly the situations users find most natural.
ELLA is designed to select a handler from two inputs: the **intent** of the message and the **state of the conversation**. Lexical overlap with a command is weak evidence on its own.

The cost of an error is asymmetric. A false positive runs a specialized behavior the user never asked for, while a missed match usually costs one more message. Routing is tuned with that asymmetry in mind.
When a reference cannot be resolved there are two failure modes: ask, or guess. Asking costs one round trip. Guessing risks a wrong action and a loss of trust.
The design prefers the **clarifying question** whenever the ambiguity changes which handler should run, and a plain reply when it does not.
Groups add addressing and threading problems. The assistant must decide whether it is being spoken to, which earlier message a reply refers to, and how much of the shared context is relevant.
These are routing inputs, not formatting details. Getting them wrong produces replies that are technically valid and socially wrong.
A chat assistant sits in front of third-party services that fail: model providers, media sources, storage. The contract is that an operation is reported as complete only when it **completed**.
A plain error is preferable to a confident message describing something that did not happen. The first is recoverable by the user, and the second is a silent data-integrity problem.

Awareness of Nigerian English and Pidgin matters for routing as much as for tone, because the same sentence can mean different things depending on how it is written. A router that misreads the message cannot choose the right handler, however good the handlers are.

Voice and call work is maintained separately from production behavior and is not presented as available until it is verified. Developer and administrative controls are likewise separated from the user-facing surface.
This note describes design priorities. It makes no claim about test results.

title: Designing a status check that does not cry wolf
lede: How the live Live, Down and Status unavailable chips on this site decide what to say.

figure.caption: Two independent requests feed a three-valued verdict. Inconclusive evidence is never reported as down.

p: Next to each deployed project the site shows **Live**, **Down** or **Status unavailable**. The check measures one thing: whether the deployed site answers an HTTP request. It does not measure whether the backend behind that site works, and the labels are worded to say so.

sections.h: Why the check runs on the server
p: A browser may not read the status of another origin unless that origin sends the right cross-origin headers. Each project therefore has a small serverless function on this site that makes the request and returns a short JSON verdict.
The browser only talks to its own origin, which removes the cross-origin problem and keeps the logic in one place.
Each function requests exactly one hard-coded address. Nothing in the incoming request, such as a query parameter, can change the target.
That removes the class of **server-side request forgery** problems an open endpoint that fetches any URL would create. The functions also accept only GET and HEAD and answer anything else with 405.

Every check issues two requests with a nine second timeout. A response below 500 counts as live, including redirects and 404 pages, because the host answered. Two server errors count as down. Everything else is reported as unknown, including timeouts, network errors and mixed results.
The verdict function is a pure mapping from two observations to one of three values, which is what makes it easy to test.

Free hosting tiers sleep when idle. The first request after a quiet period can time out while the service wakes. Reporting that as down would be a **false alarm**, so inconclusive evidence is shown as Status unavailable.
A monitor that raises alarms it cannot justify trains people to ignore it.

Responses are sent with no-store, so each answer reflects the moment of the check. The page asks again every minute while the tab is visible and stops while it is hidden, which keeps load proportional to attention.

The decision logic has unit tests that mock the network and cover live, down, timeout, mixed and rejected-method cases for each endpoint. A browser test serves the site, stubs the endpoints and asserts that every chip reads Live, Down and Status unavailable correctly, including when the endpoint itself fails.

title: How this portfolio is built
lede: A static site with a readable build step, content as data and guardrails that run on every change.

figure.caption: Pages are generated from data, committed as plain files and served as static assets.

p: The site is plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript. A single Python script that uses only the standard library generates every page from JSON content files. There is no framework runtime to hydrate and no bundler to configure, so what is deployed is what is committed.

Projects, technologies, design notes and the landing page live under content/. The generator renders them into pages, a sitemap and a robots file, and project pages share one template. Adding a project means editing **data**, not markup.

The build fails if an em or en dash appears in any generated page. A browser test visits every page at four viewport widths and checks for console errors, horizontal overflow, undersized tap targets and broken internal links.
Constraints that are checked by machines stay true after the tenth edit.

The content is in the HTML. Animation, the project rail, the typed code and the pinned scroll story are layered on by script and by newer CSS features, and each falls back to a plain layout when it is unavailable, including with JavaScript off.

Animation uses transform and opacity, runs only while an element is visible, and respects the **reduced-motion** preference. Scroll-linked effects share one throttled listener and an IntersectionObserver, so the cost does not grow with the number of animated elements.

sections.h: Contact details stay out of the markup
p: Email, WhatsApp and social links are assembled in the browser, so the HTML source carries no readable contact details. This reduces casual scraping and does not claim to be a security boundary.
A push to a branch produces a Vercel preview. Merging to main publishes. The status functions deploy alongside the pages and are covered by their own unit tests.
